exercises.audioText:
N: Listen to a nurse giving a handoff report to the next shift.
Nurse: Room 204, Mr. Thompson, admitted yesterday with pneumonia. He completed his first dose of IV antibiotics at six p.m. and tolerated it well. His temperature this morning was 37.8, down from 38.5 yesterday. He is still on oxygen at two liters, and his saturation is holding at 96 percent. He can eat soft foods but has had a reduced appetite. The main concern is his mobility — he is at risk of falls, so please ensure the bed alarm is on and assist him to the bathroom. His wife will visit at seven. That is all for now.
N: Now answer the questions.
exercises.question: Why was Mr. Thompson admitted to the hospital?

exercises.audioText: Many people underestimate how much stress affects the immune system. Chronic stress can increase inflammation and make the body more vulnerable to illness. Simple habits, like regular exercise and consistent sleep schedules, can significantly reduce this risk. Today we will look at a few techniques you can start using this week.
exercises.question: What is the speaker's main point?
options: Stress can weaken the immune system
Inflammation is not related to health

exercises.audioText:
N: Listen to a conversation at a clinic reception desk.
Receptionist: Good morning, how can I help you?
Patient: I had a blood test last Thursday, and I’m calling to ask if the results are ready.
Receptionist: Let me check. Yes, the doctor reviewed them this morning. She’d like you to come in tomorrow at ten to discuss them.
Patient: Is everything okay? Should I be worried?
Receptionist: The note just says she wants to explain the results in person. It doesn’t look urgent — otherwise she would have called you directly.
Patient: Okay, I’ll be there at ten. Do I need to bring anything?
Receptionist: Just your ID and a list of any medications you’re currently taking.
N: Now answer the questions.
exercises.question: Why does the doctor want to see the patient?
options: To explain the blood test results in person.
exercises.explanation: The doctor reviewed the blood test and wants to discuss the results in person tomorrow at ten.

exercises.audioText:
N: Listen to a doctor talking to a patient during a follow-up visit.
Doctor: Your blood pressure is lower than last month — that’s good progress. It looks like the new medication is working. How are you feeling?
Patient: Better, but I still get a little dizzy in the mornings.
Doctor: That can be a side effect at first. Try taking the pill in the evening instead, and keep checking your pressure daily. If the dizziness continues for more than a week, call the clinic.
Patient: Should I still avoid salty foods?
Doctor: Yes, keep limiting salt and keep walking thirty minutes a day. Let’s meet again in two weeks.
N: Now answer the questions.
exercises.question: What positive change does the doctor mention?
options: The patient’s blood pressure has decreased.
The patient no longer needs medication.
exercises.explanation: Doctor says blood pressure is lower than last month — good progress, medication is working.

exercises.audioText: This free workshop will introduce simple ways to make daily meals more balanced. It is not a medical consultation, and participants should speak to a healthcare professional about personal concerns. Recipes and a shopping guide will be provided at the end.
